authors: Philippe Aghion, Nick Bloom, Richard Blundell, Rachel Griffith, Peter Howitt
title: Competition and Innovation: An Inverted-U Relationship
geography_period: UK firms (patents at the US patent office)
method: Schumpeterian growth model plus panel estimates of patenting on product-market competition (Lerner index) (identification draws on policy-driven changes in competition)
finding: Model and data both show an inverted-U: innovation rises with competition at low levels and falls at high levels; the inverted-U is steeper in 'neck-and-neck' industries where firms are technologically close.
summary_plain: More competition boosts innovation up to a point, after which it can dampen it. Whether a rule that increases competition helps innovation depends on how competitive the market already is.
relevance: The DMA's premise is that gatekeeper markets sit on the low-competition side of the curve, where opening them up should raise innovation.
caveats: Core evidence from UK manufacturing patents; later replications find the shape sensitive to specification.

title: The influence of regulations on innovation: A quantitative assessment for OECD countries
method: Country panel regressions of innovation indicators on economic, social and institutional regulation indices (OECD taxonomy), within an endogenous-growth framework
finding: Effects depend on the type of regulation and differ between short and long run; general legal framework quality, efficient IP regimes, unrestricted price setting, product/service legislation and environmental laws are associated with more innovation.
summary_plain: Regulation is not one thing: some kinds of rules go with more innovation and others with less. Clear legal frameworks and product rules can help innovation, while heavy-handed economic controls tend to hurt it.
relevance: Supports judging EU digital instruments by type and design rather than by the overall number of rules.
caveats: Small country panel, correlational; survey-based regulation indices.

authors: Stefan Ambec, Mark A. Cohen, Stewart Elgie, Paul Lanoie
title: The Porter Hypothesis at 20: Can Environmental Regulation Enhance Innovation and Competitiveness?
venue: Review of Environmental Economics and Policy 7(1): 2-22
method: Review of theory and empirical tests of the Porter hypothesis (Porter and van der Linde 1995, JEP 9(4)) and its 'weak', 'narrow' and 'strong' versions
finding: Evidence that well-designed (especially flexible, market-based) regulation spurs innovation (weak version) is fairly strong; evidence that it raises overall firm competitiveness (strong version) remains mixed.
summary_plain: The idea that smart regulation can push firms to innovate and even become more competitive has some support. Rules often trigger new inventions, but whether firms end up better off overall is less clear.
relevance: The main theoretical argument for regulation-induced innovation, often invoked for EU digital rules (e.g. privacy-enhancing technologies).
caveats: Evidence base is environmental, not digital; transfer to data and platform rules is by analogy.

title: Innovation under regulatory uncertainty: Evidence from medical technology
geography_period: US FDA high-risk medical device approvals (multi-decade sample)
method: Comparison of approval times for pioneer vs follow-on entrants within device categories, and before/after publication of FDA guidance documents
finding: Pioneer device entrants spend 34% (7.2 months) longer in regulatory approval than follow-on entrants, a cost upwards of 7% of bringing a new high-risk device to market; delays reflect regulatory uncertainty, and fall when objective guidance is published.
summary_plain: First movers pay a price when the rules are unclear: the earliest new medical devices took months longer to approve. Clear official guidance cut those delays.
relevance: New EU digital rules (DMA, AI Act) create similar uncertainty for first movers; guidance and specification decisions can lower it.
caveats: Medical devices, US; magnitudes not directly transferable to digital markets.

title: The False Choice Between Digital Regulation and Innovation
method: Legal and institutional analysis (law review article), no new econometrics
finding: Argues the US-EU tech gap is not explained by strict EU digital regulation but by deeper factors: fragmented digital single market, shallow capital markets, punitive bankruptcy law, risk-averse culture, and weaker ability to attract global talent.
summary_plain: Europe's lag in tech is mostly not caused by its digital rules. Missing venture capital, a fragmented market and harsh failure laws matter more.
relevance: The leading counter-argument to claims that EU digital rules explain Europe's innovation gap.
caveats: Argumentative synthesis, not causal estimation; author is a prominent scholar of EU regulatory influence.

authors: Jian Jia, Ginger Zhe Jin, Liad Wagman
title: The Short-Run Effects of the General Data Protection Regulation on Technology Venture Investment
geography_period: EU vs US and rest of world tech ventures, 2014-2019
method: Difference-in-differences around GDPR enforcement (May 2018), EU ventures vs US/rest-of-world ventures, Crunchbase and VentureXpert data
finding: Negative post-GDPR effects on EU ventures in the number of deals, total dollars raised and dollars per deal; the INFORMS release reports a 26.1% reduction in monthly deals for EU ventures relative to US ventures in the first year.
summary_plain: After GDPR, European tech start-ups raised less venture money and closed fewer deals than comparable US start-ups. The study only covers the first year.
relevance: Direct evidence that a major EU digital regulation can reduce early-stage investment in European tech.
caveats: Short window (under one year post); confounding with other 2018 EU-US shocks hard to rule out.

title: Privacy Regulation and Online Advertising
geography_period: EU vs non-EU countries, 2000s (around the ePrivacy Directive)
method: Difference-in-differences on randomized ad-exposure field tests (3.3 million respondents, 9,596 campaigns) around the EU ePrivacy Directive
finding: After the EU privacy laws, display ads became far less effective at changing stated purchase intent relative to other countries, an average reduction of about 65%, concentrated on general-content sites and plain banner ads.
summary_plain: Once EU rules limited tracking, online ads in Europe became much less effective. That hits the revenue model of free websites such as news sites.
relevance: Early causal evidence that EU data rules shift economics of ad-funded digital services, a mechanism also relevant for DMA data-combination limits.
caveats: Outcome is stated purchase intent, not sales; pre-GDPR regime.

title: Economic Research on Privacy Regulation: Lessons from the GDPR and Beyond
method: Survey of the empirical economics literature on the GDPR
finding: The literature has largely, though not universally, documented harms to firms (performance, innovation, competition, the web, marketing), alongside some objective privacy improvements; identification is hard because of weak control groups, uneven compliance and changed data observability.
summary_plain: Most studies find GDPR imposed costs on businesses, but some show real privacy gains. Measuring the benefits is much harder than measuring the costs.
relevance: The best single overview of how a flagship EU digital regulation affected firms and innovation.
caveats: Working paper; consumer-benefit side under-measured by construction.

authors: Garrett A. Johnson, Scott K. Shriver, Samuel G. Goldberg
title: Privacy and Market Concentration: Intended and Unintended Consequences of the GDPR
method: Panel event study of website vendor use for EU vs non-EU users around GDPR enforcement
finding: The week after enforcement, website use of web technology vendors fell 15% for EU residents and vendor-market concentration rose 17%, with Google and Facebook vendors gaining relative share; aggregate changes dissipated by end-2018 but persisted in advertising.
summary_plain: GDPR cut websites' use of data vendors but helped the biggest players, Google and Facebook, gain share. Privacy rules can unintentionally strengthen dominant firms.
relevance: Shows how compliance costs can entrench gatekeepers, a tension the DMA aims to correct.
caveats: Mostly short-run; effects faded for aggregate measures.
interested_party: Acknowledges funding from the Marketing Science Institute and the George Mason University Program on Economics & Privacy (which has received tech-industry funding)

authors: Christian Peukert, Stefan Bechtold, Michail Batikas, Tobias Kretschmer
title: Regulatory Spillovers and Data Governance: Evidence from the GDPR
method: Difference-in-differences on third-party HTTP requests, 12 months before and 6 months after GDPR, comparing sites by exposure to EU law
finding: Websites substantially reduced interactions with web technology vendors, including sites not legally bound by GDPR, especially less popular sites; all vendors lost, but Google lost relatively less and gained market share in advertising and analytics.
summary_plain: GDPR changed how websites worldwide use data, even outside Europe. Smaller vendors lost out while Google gained ground.
relevance: Evidence of the 'Brussels effect' and of concentration side-effects from EU digital rules.
caveats: Measures data flows, not welfare or innovation directly.

authors: Carl Benedikt Frey, Giorgio Presidente (earlier working-paper version with Chinchih Chen)
title: Privacy regulation and firm performance: Estimating the GDPR effect globally
geography_period: Global firms with varying EU exposure, around 2018
method: Difference-in-differences by firm exposure to EU markets with firm and country-industry-year fixed effects
finding: GDPR lowered the profitability of firms targeting European consumers through a cost channel: technology firms saw a 2.1% decline in profits but not in sales; GDPR raised extra expenses and wage bills, accelerated patenting in GDPR-related fields, and burdens fell mainly on smaller firms.
summary_plain: GDPR raised costs and cut profits for firms selling to Europeans, hitting smaller companies hardest. It also spurred new privacy-related inventions.
relevance: Quantifies compliance costs and their uneven incidence by firm size, while also showing regulation-induced innovation.
caveats: Exposure-based design; profit effects modest and heterogeneous; earlier WP figures differ from published abstract.

authors: Rebecca Janssen, Reinhold Kesler, Michael E. Kummer, Joel Waldfogel
title: GDPR and the Lost Generation of Innovative Apps
method: Event study of app exit and entry around GDPR plus a structural model of demand and entry for counterfactual equilibria
finding: GDPR induced the exit of about a third of available apps and halved new app entry in the following quarters; in the long-run counterfactual GDPR reduces consumer surplus and aggregate app usage by about a third.
summary_plain: After GDPR, many apps disappeared and far fewer new ones launched. The authors estimate users lost a lot of value from the missing apps.
relevance: Among the largest estimated innovation costs of an EU digital regulation, relevant to cumulative compliance burdens on small developers.
caveats: Global app store with no clean non-GDPR control; welfare relies on structural assumptions; privacy benefits not valued.

authors: Colleen Cunningham, Florian Ederer, Song Ma
title: Killer Acquisitions
method: Theory plus difference-in-differences comparing development of acquired drug projects that overlap vs do not overlap with acquirer's portfolio
finding: Acquired projects are less likely to be developed when they overlap with the acquirer's portfolio, especially where the acquirer has market power; conservatively 5.3%-7.4% of acquisitions in the sample are killer acquisitions.
summary_plain: Some big firms buy up start-ups to shut down rival products. Weak competition oversight can therefore cost innovation.
relevance: Underpins DMA Article 14 merger-notification duties for gatekeepers: lax regulation can also harm innovation.
caveats: Pharma, not digital; mechanism in tech is debated.

authors: Sai Krishna Kamepalli, Raghuram Rajan, Luigi Zingales
title: Kill Zone
method: Theoretical model of platform competition, app developer adoption and VC financing under expected acquisition
finding: The prospect of quick acquisition by an incumbent platform reduces app developers' incentive to adopt an entrant, lowering the entrant's stand-alone value and acquisition price, and so reducing VC incentives to fund entry: a 'kill zone' around incumbents.
summary_plain: When start-ups expect to be bought by a tech giant, fewer users and partners back them and investors fund fewer of them. Unchecked platform power can choke off innovation.
relevance: Theoretical case that ex-ante platform regulation such as the DMA could raise start-up investment rather than reduce it.
caveats: Theory; empirical support for kill zones is limited and contested.
